author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.




Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.




After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.




The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.




The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.

author: Mada Masr
title: Mada Masr to challenge constitutionality of media law in Lina Attalah’s first court hearing
content:
During the first session in Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah’s trial on Tuesday morning, her defense counsel is to petition the court for access to evidence in the case, including documentation held by media regulators regarding the applications for a license that the organization has repeatedly filed since 2018.




It will also challenge the constitutionality of articles in the law regulating the press, requesting that the case file be referred to the Supreme Constitutional Court or that the defense counsel be granted authorization to file its own case before the court.




Attalah is present at the New Cairo misdemeanor court to attend the first hearing in her trial on charges of establishing, managing and operating a website without a license, following her investigation by the Supreme State Security Prosecution on October 21.




Lawyers are also set to attend the New Cairo court session on behalf of the Journalists Syndicate, which said on Monday that it has submitted a formal memorandum to the Supreme Media Regulatory Council “regarding the crisis over Mada Masr’s license application and the legal action linked to it.”




The memo stresses that there were violations of due process in the administrative handling of Mada Masr’s licensing application, that Mada Masr was not notified of the decision and that the proper recourse is “a challenge before the administrative judiciary rather than criminal prosecution,” according to a statement issued on Monday evening by syndicate head Khaled al-Balshy, which Mada Masr reviewed.




The syndicate’s lawyers are to submit a legal memorandum to the court during the Tuesday session in support of Mada Masr, based on arguments laid out in their memo to the SMRC.




More broadly, the syndicate called for a review of the licensing rules, as stated by Balshy.




The Supreme State Security Prosecution referred Attalah to the court on Thursday, less than 24 hours after questioning her on charges of running a website without a license and of publishing false news, with the latter accusation dropped from the charge sheet in the trial referral.




Lawyer Hassan al-Azhari, Mada Masr’s legal counsel, 

described 

the “haste” in the referral and its scheduling as “unjustified urgency,” given the absence of circumstances in the case that require rapid resolution.




During trial proceedings, the defense counsel will seek from the court full access to evidence in the case, including the facts of the licensing procedures and related notifications, details of the charges Attalah is accused of and the time period over which it is alleged that the crime took place.




The defense team is also set to ask the court to grant them access to the full case file and to request that the court access all documentation regarding Mada Masr’s licensing application held by the SMRC.




It will request that the original SMRC notification rejecting Mada Masr’s license, which was not delivered to the organization, be brought before the court. The defense counsel will challenge the claim that Attalah received notice of rejection decision, requesting proof of its receipt.




Mada Masr has applied on multiple occasions since 2018 for a license to operate, when a new law organizing the media and the press was 

passed

, resubmitting its application 2020 upon the issuance of its bylaws.




It received no response from the regulatory council at the time. Instead, Attalah was informed by prosecutors, during a separate interrogation she was summoned to in 2022, that the SMRC had rejected the organization’s license application. Mada Masr responded by filing a lawsuit challenging the council’s failure to notify it of its decision.




Mada Masr will submit a memorandum to the court challenging the constitutionality of Articles 6 and 105 of Law 180/2018 Regulating the Press, the Media and the SMRC, arguing that they violate seven articles of the 

Constitution

: 65, 70, 71, 92, 95, 96 and 211.




In light of this, the defense is asking that the court either suspend the case and refer it to the Supreme Constitutional Court or that it permit the lawyers to file a case before the constitutional court themselves to seek a ruling on whether the two articles of the media law are consistent with the constitutional provisions specified.




Article 6 of the media law states that “websites may not be established or managed in the Arab Republic of Egypt, nor may offices or branches of websites operating from outside the country be managed, except after obtaining a license from the supreme council in accordance with the rules and conditions it sets in this regard.” For a breach of that article, the council may take the prescribed measures, including license cancellation, suspension of website activity or blocking where there is no valid license. The article provides for the council’s licensing decisions to be challenged before the administrative court.




Article 105 sets out penalties for violating certain provisions of the same law: a fine of LE1 to LE3 million, along with the closure and confiscation of equipment and devices. In a repeat offense, the article says, both the minimum and maximum penalty are doubled.

The post 

Mada Masr to challenge constitutionality of media law in Lina Attalah’s first court hearing

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

author: Mada Masr
title: Parliament gives Sisi mandate to back Saudi Arabia militarily, opposition rejects ‘blank-check authorization’
content:
Parliament authorized President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to “take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, following coordination between the two countries, to defend its territory, sovereignty and holy sites against any external attacks,” 

according 

to a statement issued by House of Representatives Speaker Hesham Badawy.




Lawmakers in the House, who had gathered for the third-closed door session on the matter in proceedings that began over an hour later than planned, stood in order to vote in support of the authorization, with a majority of two-thirds casting their votes in favor.




Twelve lawmakers from the Egyptian Social Democratic Party, along with four other opposition MPs — Diaa Dawoud, Atef Maghawry, Ahmed Farghaly and Abdel Alim Dawoud — refused to endorse the mandate, remaining seated during the vote, according to two parliamentary sources who spoke separately to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity. Lawmakers from pro-government parties voted in favor, they added.




Riyadh has made no official public statement, neither on Sisi’s request for parliamentary authorization nor on Parliament’s approval of it. Badawy’s statement, however, used the phrase “following coordination between the two countries,” instead of “if we are asked to do so,” the phrase Sisi 

used 

when he asked for the mandate earlier this month.




Saudi daily Okaz 

used

 Badawy’s formulation in its commentary on the decision, which it said “comes within the framework of Egyptian-Saudi coordination on the security challenges facing the region.”




One of the parliamentary sources said that Badawy did not open any of the three sessions by reading out the proposed measure or the relevant constitutional provision, as is customary when Parliament considers a presidential decree, agreement or similar measure. Instead, he merely 

asked 

lawmakers to indicate their positions and vote on authorizing the president to take “defensive measures” to protect Saudi Arabia if Riyadh requested them, he added.




The same source stressed that parliamentary custom requires that lawmakers be given specific details — not shared with the press — including the nature of any mission assigned to Egyptian military forces that are to operate abroad, the size and composition of the force and the mission’s duration. None of these details was presented during the sessions, the source said. Instead, Parliament only gave the president authority to act in coordination with Saudi Arabia, he added.




The Constitution requires parliamentary approval when troops are sent on a combat mission outside the borders, making it necessary to provide lawmakers with basic information about the mission, the source said. Granting the president “blank-check authorization,” the source argued, is a contentious issue.




Egyptian Social Democratic Party member Freddy al-Bayady likewise told Mada Masr that no details were presented in either of the two previous sessions, as well as in Monday’s, on the nature and limits of the military mission, the duration and scope of the authorization, its financial and human risk or the risk of the conflict widening and affecting Red Sea and Suez Canal navigation. 




Bayady holds a seat in the House, butunable to attend Monday’s session as he was out of the country, he told Mada Masr.




He stressed that his party’s MPs stand in solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reject attacks on its territory, but need enough information to make a decision after weighing the consequences.




Egypt has previously provided military support to Saudi Arabia during Operation Decisive Storm in 2015, and to the United Arab Emirates earlier this year, without putting the matter before Parliament, the parliamentary source noted.




In their viewpoint, bringing the matter before Parliament this time indicates that the planned support could go beyond a limited deployment of equipment or troops, something that he argued compelled the state to seek out parliamentary approval this time.




Article 152 of the Constitution 

requires 

the president to consult the National Defense Council before declaring war or sending armed forces on combat missions outside the country. It also requires approval from two-thirds of the members of the House, voting in a closed session under Article 130 of the House’s bylaws.




In May, Egypt sent a “

detachment

” — a limited military formation drawn from one or several corps — to the UAE. Sources at the time said that the word “detachment” came to “signal the limited size of the formation and the limited duration of the presence,” a gesture of Egyptian support for the UAE against Iranian attacks that stopped short of real Egyptian involvement in the war.




Before that, Egypt had taken part in Operation Decisive Storm, the coalition that Saudi Arabia has led in Yemen since 2015. It 

dispatched 

four naval vessels to secure the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the Gulf of Aden, alongside air force participation. Cairo 

said 

at the time that it is prepared to send ground troops “if the situation warrants,” but it never did.




On October 17, Sisi called for an emergency parliamentary session during the Egyptian Military Academy graduation ceremony, asking lawmakers to authorize him to take any measures necessary to protect Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks “if we are asked to do so.”




“We are not looking for a role to play, but it makes no sense whatsoever for us to allow any harm to come to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its security or its stability,” he said during the ceremony.




He appealed to “everyone in the Gulf” to stop the war. “Regardless of this appeal, whether it is heeded or not, Egypt, in line with His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohamed bin Salman’s directives, will carry out any measure to protect and defend you,” he added.




The president stressed that he is not speaking “in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. We are speaking only in defense.”




After Sisi’s remarks, House Speaker Hesham Badawy called an emergency plenary session for the following morning. 




Before Parliament convened on October 18, the presidential spokesperson 

announced

 three points agreed upon by the National Defense Council at a meeting chaired by Sisi earlier that day. The council declared Egypt’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia, out of a belief that Saudi national security is tied to Egyptian and Arab national security, and pledged to provide the country with all necessary and available forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources and territorial integrity and safeguard Islamic holy sites.




The council also called for continued and intensified political and diplomatic efforts, in coordination with relevant regional and international parties, to de-escalate tensions across the region and peacefully resolve the crisis affecting it.




Then, Parliament held a three-hour closed-door session before postponing a final decision. The vote was deferred to sessions scheduled for October 19 and 20. On October 19, however, lawmakers postponed the vote again until Monday, citing the need to give all MPs an opportunity to express their views.




As Parliament held its first session last week, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, Ahmed al-Tayeb, 

called 

for the urgent formation of a mediation committee comprising respected, wise figures from Arab and Muslim countries. The committee, he said, should work to halt armed conflicts across the region and bridge differences between the parties involved. He expressed his readiness to support its efforts but stopped short of explicitly opposing Egyptian military defense measures to protect Saudi Arabia.




In a new statement, Tayeb 

condemned

 on Monday morning the Houthi attacks on Mecca, Madinah and Saudi civilian infrastructure, calling for them to stop and renewed his appeal for the committee’s formation.




With Parliament’s decision still pending, Foreign Minister Badr Abdel Atty and General Intelligence Service chief Hassan Rashad 

traveled

 to Riyadh on October 21, where they met Crown Prince Mohamed bin Salman and delivered a message from Sisi to King Salman bin Abdel Aziz. 

According 

to Abdel Atty, the message reaffirmed Egypt’s support for Saudi Arabia in the face of the attacks while stressing the need to seek a political solution to the crisis.




Earlier that day, Sisi had also 

said 

that any Egyptian military support for Saudi Arabia would be aimed at protecting the kingdom’s territory and borders, not launching attacks on Yemen.




The Saudi-Houthi front is witnessing its most violent 

escalation 

since the collapse of the truce that had held since 2022.




On Monday, the Houthis 

said 

they attacked oil pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline and Riyadh airport. The Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, announced that it destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, one of which it said had been used to fire a missile toward Riyadh.




According to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium published on Monday, around 86 percent of scheduled flights at King Khalid International Airport were canceled between October 8 and October 25.




In July, the Houthis declared a “naval blockade” of the kingdom and attacked Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. In September, they launched a ground attack, capturing the Yemeni Port of Mokha, which had been under the control of the Saudi-led coalition’s joint forces, effectively controlling Bab al-Mandab. By early October, the two sides were escalating: the internationally recognized Yemeni government launched the Fajr al-Yemen Operation to retake Sanaa, backed by extensive Saudi air support, while the Houthis attacked facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco and 

struck

 King Khalid International Airport, killing 12 people and wounding hundreds.

The post 

Parliament gives Sisi mandate to back Saudi Arabia militarily, opposition rejects ‘blank-check authorization’

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

title: St. Catherine Monastery’s land ownership lawsuits adjourned after archbishop backs Egypt-Greece deal
content:
St. Catherine’s Monastery’s archbishop said on Saturday that he intends to sign an agreement with the Egyptian government that would organize the religious community’s relationship to the monastery and surrounding lands where they have based their spiritual life for over 1,400 years.




Egypt’s government had put forward a draft proposal in July that would consolidate ownership of the monastery and surrounding lands in the hands of the Egyptian state for the first time, following decades of dispute over the status of the religious sanctuary in South Sinai, which has effectively been independent of state and legal frameworks, since its history at the site predates these frameworks’ jurisdiction.




The dispute had escalated when the Ismailia Court of Appeals 

issued

 a 2025 ruling establishing the state’s ownership of the monastery lands, granting the monastery’s usufruct rights to occupy and manage a majority of the property but ordering the expulsion of the monastery’s then-archbishop from a portion of the lands on the grounds that he had seized them unlawfully. The ruling precipitated a series of competing claims to the monastery and its lands and a crisis over the monastery’s leadership. author: Mada Masr
title: Maybe, tomorrow
content:
On a good week, our job feels like the ideal job. You don’t need to wrestle with making sense of the big picture and then pull a break to focus on your own life. Your life is all about trying to make sense with and for everyone around you, and to do so, you summon your tools, nourish them, sharpen them. These include looking for the facts, especially the hidden ones. You sift through material, you speak to sources, you go back to the material in ongoing loops. You need the history to draw the context. It changes all understanding of facts. You need the social sciences to read the data critically. You need the aesthetics of form to weave the story and start journeying it to the public. You need some philosophy for the whole thing to come together, because there is just a lot of paradox. You are also tempering a little with time, because understanding might instruct a thing or two for tomorrow. 




Isn’t one fortunate, theoretically speaking, to be a journalist? We know you might not agree with us.




This past week would have been an ideal one for all the above. First, the president announced, for the first time in Egyptian modern history, what was widely read as a serious intention for a transition of power by the end of this term. with Egypt’s looming intervention

title: Organizations rally in support of Mada Masr, condemn ‘weaponization’ of media law against independent journalism
content:
Rallying in support of Mada Masr, statements of solidarity have emerged in recent days from domestic and international advocacy organizations, political figures and parties, journalists and media platforms, all expressing their backing for the independent journalistic website and for Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah, following her referral to trial last week by prosecutors.




Though Mada Masr has been called in for questioning on an almost annual basis in relation to journalistic coverage, this is the first time prosecutors initiate a trial of this kind. Attalah is due to attend a misdemeanor court session in New Cairo on Tuesday on the charges of founding, managing and operating a website without a license.




During a gathering at the Journalists Syndicate on Saturday, several General Assembly members and independent journalists declared their support for Mada Masr and condemned what they described as an “assault on independent journalism,” referring to the escalation that began in September with the arrest of six journalists from the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh.

title: Khartoum courts UN-backed relief to stave off truce pressure; Tasis govt heedful after health minister’s angry exit; Abyei strike tests Juba ties; Drones hit RSF, military’s seats of power; RSF pushes in Kurmuk, military wins Geisan ground
content:

here

.




From Khartoum and Nyala, to a gold mine in South Kordofan, a town in West Kordofan and a power station in White Nile, drones tore through Sudan this week, killing hundreds and destroying homes, livelihoods and critical infrastructure.




Both sides traded blame, and each pointed to neighbors it said let the drones through. Some strikes went unclaimed, but silence from the military over its attack on the disputed Abyei region didn’t stop Juba from summoning Sudan’s ambassador on the same day to warn of a “dangerous development” in a border territory already straining relations between the two countries. Khartoum weighed in days later, with a Foreign Ministry statement denying the military was involved.




The strike on the RSF-held Naam market in Abyei set fuel depots burning. The fires were still consuming the area as the death toll exceeded 150 and thousands were displaced, and residents took to the streets in protest, activists and Abyei administration sources said.

author: Omar Refaat
title: The caretakers
content:
Cairo – Summer 2025




Between the neck and the sword  




Yet, we go on, somehow, somewhen, somewhere. 




What’s making the unbearable bearable then? Who’s trying to make the fractured whole, the  paralysis somehow silently fruitful? Who’s trying to make the harshness of fate, hard not to adore and hard not to loathe fate, a feather more healthy? Who’s trying to reframe, to salvage, our maimed context on the run? 




Who, unsung, has been taking care of some of us in this beautiful brutal Cairo the past few, calamitous years? 




I looked around me and asked myself. 




What is love, in other words, and how is it being dispensed in the moonless waves of this incomprehensible grief?




What does love look like in the mutilated, public square now, mauled by this hellish, false reality shoved down our parched throats? What mermaid shapes is it taking in the fissures? In the plague of small, deranged men let loose on us, where does love drip, bloom calmly, lucidly, on its own? And we’re not even seeing it in the blur of our unfathomable resignation. Where do we, the afflicted of this earth, hold on, and who do we hold on to, hold dear, in this gale? What subtle kinds of repair are plugging the leak of meaning, the love-deficit, that won’t stop gushing with a grain of sand? author: Mostafa Hosny
title: ‘Citizens’ health’ session at Egypt Forum 2026 boasts spending success with no mention of declining hospital bed numbers
content:
On Tuesday, the second day of Egypt Forum 2026, Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar described the political leadership’s support for the healthcare sector as unprecedented.




Speaking at the “citizen’s health” 

session

 of Egypt Forum 2026, he said the approach dated back to the beginning of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s presidency in 2014, when, he 

said,

 Egypt faced a massive “disease burden,” with a lack of data and years of inadequate budget allocations that had failed to meet developmental ambitions for the system, particularly as population growth accelerated.




The minister said the state’s development plan had delivered gains in the sector, citing 16 presidential initiatives that had benefited 95 million citizens at a cost of LE44 billion. 




Abdel Ghaffar stressed that success in healthcare should not be measured by spending levels, but by the results citizens ultimately experience.




Mada Masr looked into some of those results, drawing from government 

data

 published by the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS).




One clear result over the time period is the notable decline in the number of beds in public hospitals between 2013 and 2024, with a drop from around 98,291 to 84,225. 




Over the same period, the number of beds in private hospitals rose from 26,009 to 36,014.

author: Mada Masr
title: Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah referred to trial on charges of running unlicensed website
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was referred to trial on Thursday on charges of establishing and managing a website without a license, according to lawyer Hassan al-Azhari, Mada Masr’s legal counsel.




The Supreme State Security Prosecution referred Attalah to trial at a New Cairo misdemeanors court, where sessions will begin on October 27.




The referral decision came after Attallah was questioned for over six hours by prosecutors on Wednesday at the Supreme State Security Prosecution headquarters in New Cairo. Prosecutors questioned her during the session on charges of running a website without a license and of publishing false news with the aim of disturbing public peace, with the latter accusation dropped from the charge sheet in the trial referral.




Azhari described the “haste” in the trial referral, which came just hours after the interrogation closed, and its scheduling for the coming week as “unjustified urgency” given the absence of circumstances in the case that require rapid resolution.




Wednesday’s investigation, labelled Supreme State Security Prosecution Case 9072/26, comprised information and documents compiled by the National Security Agency, including a report Mada Masr published earlier this month describing a 

wave of protests in prisons after the postponement of the criminal procedures law

author: Mahmoud Bashir
title: Israeli forces arrest cancer patient, daughter returning to Gaza
content:
Israeli forces arrested two Palestinians on Tuesday evening as they were returning home to the Gaza Strip after traveling to Egypt for medical treatment, according to a statement from their family and one of their relatives who spoke to Mada Masr.




The two arrested, a cancer patient and her daughter, were among patients who were traveling both in and out of Gaza via the Rafah border crossing, which was reopened on Tuesday for the first time following its extended three-week closure by Occupation 

forces

.

 




Twenty-nine patients, along with 42 companions, 

left

 the Gaza Strip on Tuesday to receive treatment in Egyptian hospitals. Among them were critical cases, chronic disease patients and those with serious injuries. 

A group of 75 Palestinians returning to Gaza after receiving medical treatment abroad arrived via Rafah the same day to 

the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis.




The Rafah crossing, which was closed for almost two years after Israel 

occupied

 the crossing area in 2024, was 

reopened

 in February to provide passage to the sick and injured exiting Gaza for medical treatment, those returning from Egypt after completing treatment courses abroad, as well as for Palestinians who were 

stranded

 outside the strip and unable to return home amid Israel’s genocidal war.

title: Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah released by prosecutors on LE100,000 bail
content:
After investigations that lasted for over six hours, Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was ordered released by prosecutors on Wednesday evening on LE100,000 bail.




Attalah was questioned by the Supreme State Security Prosecution in Case 9072/2026 on charges of publishing false news inside and outside the country, with questions touching on a recently-published Mada Masr 

report

 concerning a wave of protest actions at a number of prisons across the country.




She was also questioned about Mada Masr’s work since its foundation, as well as about the steps its management has taken to obtain a license, according to lawyer Mokhtar Mounir.




Mada Masr has sought to obtain a license from the Supreme Media Regulatory Council (SMRC) on 

two

 

occasions

 since 2018.




On both occasions, it 

received

 no response. It was only informed of the SMRC’s rejection of the application in 2022, when Attalah was 

summoned

 for questioning in another case on charges of “running a website without the proper license.” She was presented with the rejection during that session.




Since then, Mada Masr has 

filed

 a lawsuit against the SMRC for damages incurred by its failure to inform the organization about its rejection of the application. The lawsuit was 

rejected

.

author: Mada Masr
title: Egypt Forum 2026 celebrates higher attendance at schools still struggling without teachers or classrooms
content:
Education has remained one of the main domestic fronts for the government in recent years, with chronic complaints around low spending in the sector.




At the start of the academic year in September, Education Minister Mohamed Abdel Latif faced fierce public and parliamentary pushback over controversial decisions affecting schools nationwide. 




Chief among them was the new enforcement of compulsory weekly assessments and homework, along with curriculum shakeups that drew formal parliamentary briefing requests accusing the ministry of running an evaluation regime that burns out students and teachers — who are already scarce — without improving learning.




Amid this simmering backlash, the Cabinet scrambled to stage-manage the narrative ahead of Egypt Forum 2026, a multi-day event mandated by President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on October 1 to showcase national development and institutional dialogue.




After opening a window for people to register questions and concerns for discussion at the forum, the Cabinet said that education had outpaced all other issues with more than 15,000 public inquiries submitted on the topic, reflecting the degree of public concern.




We don’t know what these public inquiries were, as they have not been published in a publicly accessible location so far.




So, what did the government choose to talk about?

author: Mada Masr
title: Youth and sports in rural areas: Greater access or declining participation?
content:
Increased state investment in youth and sports facilities was Sports Minister Gohar Nabil’s boast on the first day of the 

Egypt Forum 2026

, as part of the government’s tour of its own 

achievements

.




During a session titled “Youth and sports: From creating opportunities to making an impact,” Nabil 

pointed 

to more than LE31 billion spent on youth and sports facilities, including 4,382 youth centers, 23 sports stadiums, 40,000 youth center leagues, 12 youth and sports cities and 4,566 football pitches. He did not specify over what period those billions were spent.




Against the minister’s showpiece figures, the session made no mention of data from the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics, which show a sharp drop in the number of matches played and sports teams registered at village youth centers between 

2013

 and 

2024

, even as the number of centers went up.




According to CAPMAS’s 2013 and 2024 annual bulletins, the number of matches played by sports teams at village youth centers fell by 85.5 percent over the decade.




During the same period, the number of sports teams dropped by 50.3 percent, even though the number of centers rose by 6.7 percent.

author: Mada Masr
title: The future of rule: More questions than answers
content:
It took four days of successive presidential reiterations before the various parties began to grasp that, this time, it is different.




And no wonder. Never in Egypt’s modern history has the head of state chosen to hand power over voluntarily. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi himself 

promised

, time and again, during his first term that he would not move to amend the constitution and extend his rule. That changed at the start of his second term, when the constitution was in fact amended, and he secured two further terms, keeping him in office until 2030.




That’s why when the president opened his speech at the Armed Forces’ educational seminar on Wednesday by announcing he would not extend his rule, the confusion was plain on all sides, state institutions included.




At the seminar, Sisi said he had no intention of amending the Constitution. The audience hesitated for a few seconds before applauding. And many people 

noticed

.




The next day, he stated the announcement in clearer terms. But the statement, issued by the presidential spokesperson, was edited, changing “until 2030” into “until the last day of his rule.” There is a big difference between the two formulations. The latter preserves a measure of vagueness, which some apparently felt was needed until things became clearer.

author: Mada Masr
title: State security prosecution summons Mada Masr editor-in-chief for investigation
content:
Lina Attalah, Mada Masr’s editor-in-chief, received a summons today from the Supreme State Security Prosecution to attend a questioning session on Wednesday, October 21. The summons did not say why she is being questioned.




The new investigation, Case 9072/2026, is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr, its journalists and its editor-in-chief in the past six years. The most recent was in August 2025, when the security prosecution released Attalah on LE30,000 bail. She was questioned at the time on charges of “broadcasting false news” and “using a website without a license,” based on a National Security Agency investigation report, in relation to a Mada Masr story on prisoners’ complaints of abuse in detention facilities. 

When 

asked 

why she trusted the sources cited in the story, Attalah said she had abided by professional journalistic standards and had acted in the public interest.

 She also pointed to the legally protected right to inform authorities of events through publication, noting that the outlet presents a full range of viewpoints.

State security prosecution summons Mada Masr editor-in-chief for investigation

Mada Masr

author: Lana Harb
title: Lebanon’s ‘pilot zone’ experiment: The case of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah
content:
Ihsan Yaghi’s house in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah is scorched from the inside. Piles of rubble fill the rooms she and her husband walk through to see what remains. What was not demolished by nearby Israeli strikes has been blackened by fire, with soot covering the interior walls. But Yaghi refuses to leave.




“Despite everything, this is still my land, and we have a very strong attachment to this land that we can’t let go of,” Yaghi tells Mada Masr.




Yaghi’s is one of roughly 100 families that have, since July, returned to Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, one of around 70 villages in southern Lebanon still under Israeli occupation, its residents displaced, its homes destroyed, its fields unreachable. The question of what should be done for the south, how to rebuild and how to return people to their land under continued occupation, has become one of the most pressing political questions in Lebanon. The answer currently on offer from the Lebanese government and its international partners is the “pilot zone.”




On July 21, the United States announced 

the official commencement

 of pilot zone operations in three villages in southern Lebanon: Froun, Srifa and Zawtar al-Gharbiyah. author: Mada Masr
title: Parliament puts off vote on authorizing Sisi to send troops to Saudi Arabia until Tuesday
content:
After a closed session on Sunday that ran for nearly three hours, the House of Representatives postponed a vote on authorizing President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to send troops on a combat mission to defend Saudi Arabia, putting it off until after Monday’s and Tuesday’s sessions.




Sisi had called for an emergency parliamentary session during the Egyptian Military Academy graduation ceremony on Saturday, asking lawmakers to authorize him to take any measures necessary to protect Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks “if we are asked to do so.”




The delay came after MPs demanded details of the Armed Forces’ role in Saudi Arabia beyond the National Defense Council’s 

statement

, asking that every MP get a chance to express their views on the matter, according to three lawmakers who spoke to Mada Masr.




MP Ehab Mansour, the Egyptian Social Democratic Party parliamentary bloc head, told Mada Masr after the session that members were instructed not to share details of the discussions with the media.




“We are not looking for a role to play, but it makes no sense whatsoever for us to allow any harm to come to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its security or its stability,” Sisi said during the graduation ceremony.

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Govt scrambles to solve fuel crisis without clear end in sight, divided on fava bean import ban; Quintet tries to balance competing political initiatives; RSF continues Blue Nile push; Military sets sights on Darfur
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter

 here

.




The struggling wartime economy took center stage this week in Sudan with a pair of issues at the heart of daily life.




The first is a fuel crisis that has grown increasingly worse in recent weeks as gas stations have become makeshift campsites and prices have skyrocketed. While the government has projected an outward image of assurance, behind closed doors, the wheels are turning to try to bring fuel to the nine states under military control.




The plan has two axes, sources informed of the discussion told Mada Masr. The first is essentially a triage: tighten fuel allocations and movement to where it is needed. Various government bodies have tried their hand at centralizing authority to better streamline decision-making, but Sudan’s fractured executive apparatus has seen more attempts than results.




The second part of the plan would require solving the issue at its source: bringing in new supplies to offset the non-performing domestic oil sector. For this, Transitional Sovereignty Council chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan is holding talks with Saudi Arabia. But as an informed TSF source told Mada Masr, the government cannot commit to a timeline to end the crisis until external agreements are finalized and the necessary financial guarantees are in place.

author: Mada Masr
title: As Sisi vows to leave power by 2030, sources differ on whether he really means it
content:
Speaking at the 44th Cultural and Educational Symposium of the Egyptian Armed Forces on 

Wednesday

, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi 

said

 Egypt’s “Constitution would not be touched.”

 




His remarks came as part of a longer speech warning against a return to the demonstrations and protests that swept the country after 2011, alongside a series of other political messages, including a 

declaration

 that he 

would

 “never tire of protecting Egypt.”

 

He reiterated similar messages again on 

Thursday,

 during a speech at the Police Academy’s graduation ceremony, saying he would continue working “until the final day” of his presidential term in 2030.




With 

talk

 of lifting presidential term limits already a feature of political conversations in the leadup to the 2025 parliamentary election, a parliamentary source told Mada Masr at the time, Sisi’s comments sparked immediate queries about how long the president will remain in power.

 




Speaking on condition of anonymity, three parliamentary sources close to a sovereign security agency told Mada Masr that Sisi’s pledge not to touch the Constitution is inseparable from a broader plan to reshape the country’s political landscape, and is driven by his desire to avoid the mistakes of ousted President Hosny Mubarak, whose three decades in power fostered the widespread resentment that would lead to the 2011 revolut

author: Nadia Salem
title: ‘Revolution, the dirty word’: On Lara Baladi’s Z for Zarafa
content:
What happens after revolution? How do we remember, if we do at all?




In her exhibition, Z for Zarafa, which opened at Gypsum Gallery at the start of June and closed on September 23, Lara Baladi takes us through a scavenger hunt of moments, leading us into an archive of revolution, specifically looked at from an aftermath vantage point of movement, migration, displacement and the ultimate wrestling for freedom.




The exhibition acts as a physical installation of aspects of an online database, 

Anatomy of Revolution

, which is a project exploring the various iconography and language of resistance movements. The database 

consolidates

 research, visual, written and audio material from past and present global struggles, which Baladi gathered between 2011 and 2021 as part of her project, 

Vox Populi, Tahrir Archives

. The body of data, a vast space of references, is organized into an abecedary using the Arabic alphabet, designed to work as “an educational primer of struggles for freedom.”




The exhibition, a multi-year effort through a wide network of collaborations, brought together the works of editors, writers and visual artists reflecting on experiences of migration and exile, alongside the works of refugee women in Cairo, blacksmiths in Imbaba, antiquaries in downtown Cairo, embroiderers in Islamic Cairo and potters in Fayoum, among others.

author: Shams Eddin Essam
title: Will Supply Ministry’s wheat intervention really rein in cost of unsubsidized bread?
content:
As the grain and bakery industries petition the government for permission to increase bread prices in order to protect their profits, the Supply Ministry has 

announced

 it is injecting wheat onto the national commodity exchange to bring prices down and cut production costs.




The move came after calls for a government review of bread pricing guidelines in 

August

 and 

September

. Producers said they needed to increase consumer prices to compensate for rising production costs, particularly of flour. 

Despite talks between ministry and industry representatives, the government has held the price caps and loaf weight specifications 

steady

, announcing the supply release instead.




However, sources from the grain, milling and bakery industries who spoke to Mada Masr expressed doubt that the mechanism would meaningfully reduce production costs, indicating that the last time the ministry undertook a similar supply allocation in 2023, the move only fuelled profiteering on a secondary market that emerged in parallel to the commodity exchange.




The ministry has not said how much wheat it will offer via the commodity exchange, though ministry spokespeople 

explained

 that the extra supply would be enough to bring costs down across the supply chain.

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Ehsan Salah
title: Sudan, Egypt to pursue joint border security, as public tensions flare after deadly mine bombing
content:
In the aftermath of the bombing of a mine in the 

Halayeb Triangle

 that left scores of Sudanese miners dead, Egypt and Sudan are discussing a new security framework along the countries’ shared eastern border.

 




That framework would provide for joint coordination to pursue what both sides regard as security risks arising from organized crime, Sudanese and Egyptian officials 

told

 Mada Masr.




The push toward closer coordination comes amid public outcry in Sudan and diplomatic concern in international quarters over the killing of scores of artisanal miners in the disputed 

Halayeb Triangle

 on Saturday.

 




That public outcry was accentuated on Monday when a gunman killed two Egyptians in a main market in southern Khartoum in what Sudanese security officials involved in the investigations told Mada Masr was a retaliatory attack.




The shooting took place at around 2 pm near the 

Export Development Bank in the Local Market

, a security source in 

Khartoum State police

 told Mada Masr.

 Three Egyptians were targeted in the market’s commercial area. 

Two died at the scene, while the third was taken to the 

Omdurman Medical Corps Hospital 

for treatment.

author: Mada Masr
title: Protests at several prisons, detainee ‘banishments’ surround delay to Criminal Procedure Code
content:
A wave of protests has swept through several prisons over the last three weeks, as prisoners who were hopeful that the new Criminal Procedure Code would bring an end to their prolonged remand detention had their hopes dashed at the eleventh hour when the law’s implementation was postponed, according to several lawyers acting in defense of detainees held at different prisons who spoke separately to Mada Masr over the same time period.




The postponement pushed back what many detainees saw as a window of opportunity for authorities to release dozens of them held in remand after the law’s awaited implementation on October 1.




With that window now firmly shut until October 2027, a wave of demonstrations in detention centers has been met by security forces with measures that the lawyers say include the punitive transfer of detainees to prisons farther away from their families, a practice known as “

taghreeb”

 (banishment).




As cries and claims about the demonstrations and the security forces’ response made their way to social media, the Interior Ministry issued repeated denials that protests and abuses are taking place within prisons, most recently in an October 2 

statement

. The Public Prosecution, meanwhile, was yet to issue a statement regarding the claims at the time of publishing.

author: Mada Masr
title: State security prosecution renews detention of 6 Matsda2sh journalists for 15 days
content:
The detention of six journalists from fact-checking platform Matsda2sh was renewed for 15 days on Tuesday evening, pending further investigations, according to their lawyers. The renewal was ordered by the Supreme State Security Prosecution during today’s hearing in Case 8083/2026.




The journalists Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emaira, Abdallah Kadry, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal are being investigated in the case, registered with the Supreme State Security Prosecution, and were questioned again by prosecutors in sessions on Tuesday.




The journalists’ lawyers told Mada Masr that questioning began around 1 pm and continued into the evening at the prosecution’s headquarters in the Fifth Settlement. The sessions revisited previous lines of questioning, including questioning about wages, the managerial structure of the platform and the way work was organized, with no new evidence presented to the journalists.




All six journalists have been held at Badr 1 Prison since they were brought before the prosecution early last week. Their lawyers said they are due to receive their first family visits starting Thursday, as well as to be granted dedicated time for exercise.

author: Roaa Reda
title: From journalists’ pursuit to protection? Bid to ban jail sentences for publishing gets boost from syndicate, MPs
content:
Parliamentarians, legal advocates and representatives of the Journalists Syndicate gathered on Saturday at the Cairo syndicate headquarters for an open seminar to discuss practical steps to curb the use of detention against journalists in lawsuits related to the act of publishing.




Participants noted that, despite an explicit constitutional protection against the practice, there is a lack of mechanisms to support a change — a situation which prompted the drafting, almost a decade ago, of a law to prevent imprisonment in publishing crimes.




In an attempt to activate the dormant draft law, Tagammu Party MP Atef Maghawry told Mada Masr that he began on Monday to gather lawmakers’ support for the bill, telling Mada Masr he will seek to complete the effort over the coming weeks to secure the bill’s presentation in Parliament’s general session.




The discussion came on the back of the ongoing detention of six journalists from independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh, whose arrests earlier this month brought the number of journalists detained in relation to their work to 26.




Multiple voices at the seminar highlighted the risks facing both journalists and citizens alike given the expansion of legal grounds for the arrest of journalists over recent years.

author: Mada Masr
title: Scores killed, Sudan announces an investigation, Egypt a new phase of anti-illegal gold mining campaign
content:
In the first official comment since a mine near the Sudanese-Egyptian border was bombed on Saturday killing scores of miners, Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council 

issued

 a statement on Monday to mourn the souls of “Sudanese citizens who lost their lives in the painful incident involving a number of Sudanese miners in the border area between Sudan and the Arab Republic of Egypt.”

 




Without providing further details on when, how or where the Sudanese nationals died, the executive authority that has ruled Sudan since 2019 announced that a fact-finding committee composed of members of the Sudanese Public Prosecution as well as relevant judicial and security authorities would be formed to investigate the matter. 




The council underlined that “leadership in both brotherly countries,” referring to Egypt, have “remained in continuous communication immediately after the incident occurred, ensuring the protection of lives, preserving the relationship between the two brotherly peoples, understanding the details of the incident and sharing the facts with public opinion.”
